Content:
In general, the domain of a radical function [MATH: f(x)=\sqrt[n]{x}] depends on whether [MATH: n] (called the index) is even or odd.

Content:
If [MATH: n] is odd, then the domain of [MATH: f(x)] is always [MATH: x\in (-\infty, \infty).] For example, the domain of [MATH: f(x)= \sqrt[3]{x}] is [MATH: x\in (-\infty, \infty).]

Content:
We can see this in the graph below: the function [MATH: f(x) = \sqrt[3]{x}] extends across all values of [MATH: x.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/4549d3c5ac194ce235d2053fc943a50f]

Content:
Now, suppose that we want to find the domain of a transformed radical function, such as

Content:
[MATH: g(x)= -\sqrt[3]{-x+2}.]

Content:
The domain of [MATH: \sqrt[3]{x}] is [MATH: x\in (-\infty, \infty),] and graph transformations will not change this interval. Therefore, we conclude that the domain of [MATH: g(x)] is also [MATH: x \in (-\infty,\infty).]

items.readable_text:
Content:
Let's go back to considering [MATH: f(x)=\sqrt[n]{x}.]

Content:
If [MATH: n] is even, then the domain of [MATH: f(x)] is always [MATH: x\in [0, \infty).] For example, the domain of [MATH: f(x)= \sqrt[4]{x}\,] is [MATH: x\in [0, \infty).]

Content:
We can see this in the graph below: the function [MATH: f(x) = \sqrt[4]{x}] starts at [MATH: x=0] and extends forever to the right.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6630892e7f6ce94151a031ef58628cae]

Content:
Notice how similar this looks to the square root function! All curves of the form [MATH: y=\sqrt[n]{x}] for even [MATH: n] have this shape.

Content:
Now let's consider the function

Content:
[MATH: g(x)= 3\sqrt[4]{x+2} -2.]

Content:
To find the domain of [MATH: g(x) = 3\sqrt[4]{x+2} -2,] we proceed in exactly the same way as with square roots: we set the expression under the radical sign to be greater than or equal to zero. This gives

Content:
[MATH: x+2 \ge 0.]

Content:
Solving this inequality, we get

Content:
[MATH: x|≥ − 2.]

Content:
Therefore, the domain of [MATH: y = g(x)] is [MATH: x \in [-2, \infty).]

Content:
We can also see that this is true from the graph of the function. The graph of [MATH: y=g(x)] is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e712e5f0c118cb60c3903a7f680d4222]

Content:
In general, to find the domain of a radical function of the form [MATH: y = \sqrt[n]{f(x)},] where [MATH: n] is an even integer, we need to solve the inequality [MATH: f(x) \geq 0.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

If [MATH: n] is odd, then the domain of [MATH: f(x)] is always [MATH: x\in (-\infty, \infty).] For example, the domain of [MATH: f(x)= \sqrt[3]{x}] is [MATH: x\in (-\infty, \infty).]
